en: *The Siddham Script Record*, compiled by the Śramaṇa Zhiguang of Shan County, Mount Tai, Great Tang, based on the *Siddham Prajñābodhi* from South India. Preface:
Siddham is the script of India. The *Records of the Western Regions* states that it was devised by the Brahma King; it is the original source.
When transmitted downward, it consists of forty-seven words;
by being applied through objects, they combine to form expressions that are adapted and employed according to specific circumstances.
As these teachings flow and branch out, their source becomes increasingly vast.
While there have been slight variations in the texts according to the regions and the individuals who transmitted them,
those from Central India (Madhyadeśa) are particularly detailed and correct;
whereas in the borderlands, where customs differ, corrupt versions are also practiced.
To speak of its general outline, its fundamental source is no different;
this is the broad summary.
Recently, I have been reciting a dhāraṇī.
In his search for the original sounds and meanings, he encountered many discrepancies and errors.
It happened that a śramaṇa from South India, Prajñābodhi,
arrived bringing a Sanskrit manuscript of the dhāraṇī.
Traveling from the South Sea, he visited Mount Wutai and resided in a mountain hermitage.
Thereupon, he received [the teachings] from him;
thus, he combined the old translations of the Tang dynasty with a detailed mastery of the phonology of Central India.
There is no lack of discrepancies;
upon examining the origins and the points of conflation, they all trace back to Siddham.
The Indian monks themselves have stated this.
Shaozi studied under the former master Prajñāgupta;
he had almost exhausted the subtle nuances of the grammatical traditions.
In South India, the ancestral lineage inherited the script of Maheśvara.
This is correct; however,
the texts from Central India, which also include those from the Dragon Palace,
differ slightly from those of Southern India.
Yet their structural framework must be identical.
While the Gandhāra script is particularly distinct and unique,
the origin of its characters is entirely based on the Siddham script.
He requested that the original texts be produced so they might be examined and annotated;
he then organized their structural divisions to form chapters.
Although the pronunciations differ slightly, the literary standard remains intact.
They do not value the extraordinary in the scriptures of distant realms;
they employ the *dhāraṇīs* from the Tang records as mere approximations of Sanskrit.
How can this compare to examining the original texts themselves?
It enables students to master the Sanskrit sounds within no more than two nights;
with over seven thousand characters, it achieves its purpose with brevity and essentiality.
How sublime is the Sage’s wisdom in benefiting all beings!
Is it not here that the single character of the *dhāraṇī* contains all virtues?
Although I have not yet fully examined the various classifications within those historical records and edicts,
the application of the internal scriptures is indeed complete therein.
However, the dialects of the Five Indias vary as much as those of Chu and Xia in China.
Only now do scholars of the Central Land begin to examine and standardize them with precision.
I have thus privately recorded these archaic texts on tablets and slips; for it was said of old that the "Books of Chu" were called "Hu-wen" (barbarian script).
According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions),
the region of the Five Indias to the south of Jambudvīpa is inhabited by people of the Chu state.
The land is over ninety thousand *li* in circumference;
it borders the great ocean on three sides and has the Snow Mountains as its northern back.
At present, no Wheel-Turning King has appeared to govern it.
It is divided into more than seventy kingdoms;
collectively they are called the Five Indias,
also known as Shendu.
Some call it India;
others say it is Da-xia (Bactria).
Its people have inherited their lineage distantly from the Brahma King.
Although it is largely divided into four castes,
it is collectively called the land of the Brahmins;
therein the Buddha appeared.
It is not the land of the Hu;
however, to the north of the Snow Mountains, bordering the Pamir Range,
is where the Hu people reside.
The original forms of these characters differ [from the standard].
This is truly because their territory borders India and their written characters are intermingled;
all the sūtras and śāstras brought here follow the Indic script.
As for their customs, they imitate those [of India], though their literary style has undergone some degree of increase or diminution.
Since antiquity, many Buddhist scriptures have been sought and requested;
most of these were obtained there.
The confusion between "yu" and "lu" is simply a textual error.
Its origin is said to be Siddham,
which possesses six vowel categories.
The long and short syllables are divided into twelve characters;
they are placed at the beginning of the following chapter on capping,
where they are uttered in response to the tone to develop the rhyme.
When sounds combine according to their rhymes, syllables (*akṣara*) arise;
this refers, for example, to the short pronunciation of *a* in the rising tone (*ā*) and the long pronunciation of *a* in the level tone (*ā*), and so forth.
Among these, there are four types of characters, such as the two-syllable combination *hi-li*.
The Siddham script exists but is not employed for writing characters and is therefore omitted here.
Next, there are thirty-five phonetic characters (t'i-wén);
together with the preceding Siddham, it is clear that there are forty-seven syllables in total.
When sound is produced, the teeth, tongue, throat, and lips combine with the musical scales of *gong* and *shang*;
these have five characters each.
When combined throughout the entire vocal cavity, there are ten characters.
In this context, the three sounds *ra*, *ha*, and *la* are combined.

Regarding the character for "birth" (*janman*), it should not be applied universally across all chapters; its usage mostly belongs to the eighth [chapter], and depending on the weight of the syllable, it may or may not form a complete character, as will be discussed in detail below.
The sound of "la" (羅) is entirely absent from its generative function;
thus, in the first chapter, "tong-la-chu-zhi" (通羅除之一) means "remove one 'la' character" (the character "la" being pronounced jiàn);
in the remaining single chapters, "chu-er" (除之二) means "remove two 'ra' characters" (the two characters "ra").
These are the second, third, eighth, ninth, and tenth chapters.
Since their characters do not form a compound, they are distinguished from the first;
therefore, they are called the "remaining single chapters."
The repeated sections are excluded; three repetitions constitute a complete unit.
These refer to the four chapters beginning with the fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and those from the eleventh onwards.
The final phrases of these distinct chapters are employed for other purposes.
Furthermore, the sixth [syllable] is excluded; that is, the fifth syllable at the end of the phrase "Aṅga-ja-cha-ta-da-tāla" is used for the preceding four syllables,
and since it cannot be repeated again as a primary element, it is excluded.
Aside from those already excluded, each [syllable] is capable of generating all others; these are *ka*, *kha*, and so forth.
There are seventeen chapters of syllables.
Each character is produced approximately four hundred times, whereby the Sanskrit text becomes manifest.
Beyond the formal chapters, there are isolated and combined passages; when characters are linked together to form repetitions, these constitute the names of the characters.
There are eleven *mātrās*.
This refers to the points and strokes;
two and a half *mātrās* combined form a syllable. For the production of vowels such as *a*, *ā*, and so forth, ten *mātrās* are employed.
The dot at the side of the subsequent letter is called *visarga*, which here is pronounced with a departing tone (*qùshēng*).
It is not a *mātrā*.
A single *kriyā* (stroke) is used as a distinct *mātrā*.
The *liye* (liṅga) constitutes half the body;
the *zhīye* (śikhā) and the *jiānbǎntǐ luo* (upahṛdaya) constitute the other half.
The first chapter comprises the preceding thirty-four characters.
One calls upon the twelve vowels, beginning with *a* and *ā*,
and adds the *mātrās*; thus,
four hundred and eight syllables are produced.
This refers to the equality of the upper *ka* (𑀓) and the lower *ka* (𑀓).
The twelve characters following the sound of *ka* all take *ka* as their radical form.
By pronouncing them with the vowels such as *ā* and so forth, their *mātrās* are increased;
when combined with the phonemes and vowels, each takes on its specific form. This is illustrated by the sounds *khā*, *gā*, and so on, following the same pattern.
Thus, one chapter is completed.
The fourteen chapters that follow all take the first chapter as their model for their characters.
Each [vowel] is pronounced according to its respective increase,
joined with the consonant it corresponds to by uttering the vowels *a*, *ā*, and so forth;
subsequently, its *mātrā* (morae) are increased.
When the two characters "dang" (當) and "ti" (體) are about to merge,
one should allow them to be and not give rise to [conceptual] production;
this refers to the double "ra" (羅) in the fourth chapter.
The fifth layer consists of the syllable *vaṃ* and so forth.
The four chapters from the eleventh downward are identical to the four preceding chapters respectively, with the exception that they are excluded [from those].
In the second chapter, the syllable *jya* (祇耶) from the middle of the half-body is joined beneath the syllables *ka-ka*, etc., from the first chapter;
this is named *kī* (枳也) and *kīya* (枳耶).
There are three hundred and ninety-six characters for the generation of meanings; the character *jǐ* (枳) is pronounced as *ěr* (爾).
Now, upon close examination, it appears that *qíyé* (祗耶) should be a simplified form of the character *yé* (耶).
If this is so, it likewise avoids redundancy.
There are only three hundred and eighty-four [syllables].
Originally, the written forms numbered three hundred and ninety-six;
however, after combining *jīya* with it, *mata* was subsequently added.
In characters formed by doubling [a radical],
those below all omit the head;
the following cases are all the same.
The third chapter places the syllable *ra* beneath the syllables *ka-ka* and so forth of the first chapter;

this is called the "Three Hundred and Ninety-Six Syllables of the Abbreviated Upper Tone for *ka* and the Abbreviated Level Tone for *ka*" (the upper tone being pronounced with the force of *lì jià*).
The lower "lè" (pronounced with the *liǎo* tone) and both the upper and lower "jiā" are abbreviated;
one takes the level (*píng*) and rising (*shàng*) tones [of the respective radicals] as the sounds, and all others follow this pattern.
Chapter Four begins with the character 攞 (*la*).
Below the characters of the first chapter, it is named *kāra* (迦攞) and *kāra* (迦攞).
The total number of generated characters is three hundred and eighty-four; the character *la* (攞) is pronounced with a retroflex *l* (洛可反).
The fifth chapter contains the syllable *va*.

When combined with the syllable at the beginning of the first chapter, it is called the "Kāva" (the *kā* being aspirated and the *va* being unaspirated) syllable, numbering three hundred and eighty-four; the *va* is pronounced like the word for "room" (*fang*).
The sixth chapter joins the syllable *ma* beneath the first chapter’s syllable;
this is called *kama-kama*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four characters for generating [the syllables].
Chapter Seven will take the character *na* (曩) and join it beneath the character from the first chapter.
The name is *Kana-Kana*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four generated characters.
Chapter Eight, the half-body *Ra*.
Add the initial character of the first chapter above it;
this is called *alakālakā*.
It generates three hundred and ninety-six characters. The character *la* (勒) is pronounced with the *li* and *de* tones (as indicated by the note "the same below").
In the ninth chapter, place the syllable *raṃ* upon the letter of the second chapter;
this is named *ālkīya ālkīya*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four generated characters; if they are identical to those in the *Jñeya*, the abbreviated forms are treated the same, with repetitions removed.
Chapter Ten: Placing the semi-body syllable *ra* above the character from Chapter Three.
Namaḥ alake alake. This is the name consisting of three hundred and ninety-six syllables, abbreviated with level and rising tones.
Chapter Eleven, near its midpoint, contains the syllable *ra*.
Add these characters above the fourth chapter;
they are named *A-le-ka-la* and *A-le-ka-la*.
They produce three hundred and eighty-four characters.
The twelfth chapter contains half of the syllable *raṃ*.
When added above the syllables of the fifth chapter,
it is named *alaka-va* and *alaka-va*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four generated syllables.
In the thirteenth chapter, the semi-body syllable *ra* (𑖢) is added above the syllable from the sixth chapter.
The name is *alakṣma alakṣma*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four characters.
The fourteenth chapter, being halfway through, contains the syllable *ra*.
Add these characters above the seventh chapter;
they are named *Ālakaṇa* and *Alakaṇa*.
There are three hundred and eighty-four generated characters.
The fifteenth chapter concludes with the fifth syllable of the phrases beginning with *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, and *pa*.
Add [the respective characters] above the four characters preceding each phrase,
as well as above the final character of the first phrase and above the nine characters beginning with "ye" that follow.
The names are Aṅka, Anca, Anta, Anta, Omba, Añja, and so forth.
These certainly do not exceed twenty-nine characters.
They are not called "distinct chapters" (*varga*) because they follow the combination of rhymes;
each is pronounced using the vowels *a*, *ā*, and so forth.
There are three hundred and forty-eight characters produced [in this way], beginning with the character *aṅ* (pronounced as *ā-dǎng*).
The character 安 (ān) is pronounced with the initial *b* and the final rhyme *dǎn*;
the character 唵 (ōng) is pronounced with the initial *ā* and the final rhyme *gǎn*.
Chapter Sixteen employs the calligraphic forms of characters such as 迦 (*kā*).
By combining it with the letter *ma*, it is called *kṛ*.
There are thirty-four characters formed; alternatively, by adding the aforementioned *ma* to these, one forms additional characters for use.
It is not capable of producing [the sound] universally.
To speak according to the original letter:
now, upon careful examination, *kṛima* is simply the letter *ṛi* within the Siddham alphabet.
Chapter Seventeen: Using the Kāṭhaka and other scripts;
by combining and interchanging them, there are thirty-three characters, which receive their designations according to the texts.
This refers to those such as Aśoka and others,
each pronounced using the vowels *a*, *ā*, and so forth; thus,
three hundred and ninety-six characters are produced.

Chapter Eighteen: Beyond the primary sections, there are texts consisting of isolated or combined characters; sometimes two characters are doubled within a single entity. These are simply called "double-syllable invocations" (dahu), such as the words *duḥśatana* and others, each of which is formed through reduplication.
Alternatively, when characters of different forms are repeated, they are pronounced as a continuous stream; examples include *siddhārtha* and the like.
Or, when the *pratyaya* suffix *mat* is not present and the term stands alone as a compound, examples include words such as *sthalī*.
There are also cases where three or five [syllables] are combined;
or, although the text may consist of twelve [syllables],
the order of their radical characters is not sequential, such as in *gṛddha*, *aśvatara*, and so forth.
Alternatively, although there may be differences in weight, it is not necessarily required to call [the term] based on its weight; these are the final characters of the five phrases,
to which the initial character of the phrase is added,
and they are termed *aṅga* (limbs) and so forth, belonging to the preceding chapter.
Alternatively, there are cases where two characters are joined as a single sound,
with the written form following the sound that precedes it, such as the three-syllable compound *maṅka* and others;
these resemble what would be called *māṅka* and so forth.

Alternatively, there may be a single character with distinct names, such as the character for "sand" (沙), which has two pronunciations, *sha* and *fu* (reading *fu* as *ke*), similar to the practice of phonetic borrowing (*jiè*).
Or, one may use the script of *ma-da*.
The *ma* is further increased by its weight,
and the sound necessarily incorporates both [the preceding elements], as in the syllable *bhūm*.

This is derived from *bhrū* (with the initial *bhr-* pronounced according to the *pu-hou* rhyme) and *lū* (with the initial *l-* pronounced according to the *li-gou* rhyme), together with the eleventh *mata*.
Alternatively, there are forms that are not *maṇḍala* but serve as the decorative script for a character, such as the upward-curving crescent moon drawn above a letter.
Or, there are those that are formed but differ in their names, referring to cases where several characters combine to form a single character.
The lower character must be pronounced with its standard tone;
the middle and upper characters are combined and pronounced briefly,
without necessarily adhering strictly to their individual phonetic values.
As above, "sa" and below, "ka" are pronounced as "a-so-ka" and so forth.
There may be the sound but not the form; this refers to the section on "a-so-ka," where each character lacks the letter "a."
When reading them, one pronounces them according to their respective sounds.
Some do not derive from the characters themselves;
they exist as independent "half-body" (phonetic) graphs, such as *tadātmya* and others, which are used in practice though they have no corresponding character forms.
If there are missing characters in a word,
the term *tad* is added; however, it is pronounced with a *che* sound,
as in the case of characters such as *ka* and *kha*, where, if there is a *ta*-stroke beneath them, they are read as *jie* (pronounced *jié*) and *qiè* (pronounced *kǔ*).
Alternatively, they may originate from characters and increase in diverse forms; for instance, the character "śi" (室梨) still retains the image of "śara" (奢羅).
When these are erroneously formed into seal script, they resemble the style of *zhuàn* or *zhòu*.
Alternatively, one may examine their origins;
their forms differ from those of *kṣīra*, *kṣulla*, and so forth— which abbreviate the *ka*—
as well as from the script of *hulu* and others.
The differences between these [scripts] are like those between the *cāo* (clerical) and *lì* (seal) styles of Chinese calligraphy;
this is the grand overview of Indic scripts. The *Siddham-akṣara-nirdeśa*: 1. Na (娜) 2. Ma (麼) 3.

Sa (娑, with the upper tone) 4. Rva (囉嚩, a conjunct) 5. Śca (社若, pronounced as a conjunct) 6. Ya (也) 7. Si (悉) 8. Taṃ (曇, with the departing tone) The above is the title. Regarding the twelve vowels of *Siddham*: 1. The short vowel *A* (阿, with the upper tone), pronounced short and approximating the sound of "Ē" (惡). (Note: The characters provided in the source text represent the Siddham syllabary.)
The long *a* (ā) is pronounced with a prolonged sound; its separate form is 􇇰.
The short *i* (i) is pronounced with a rising tone, near the rhyme of *yi*; its separate form is 􇗴.
The long *i* (ī) is pronounced with a prolonged sound according to the character; its separate form is 􇗼.
The character 甌 (short) is in the third tone (shǎngshēng), its sound being close to that of 屋; it has an alternative form written as 𠇾.
The character 甌 (long) is pronounced with a long vowel; it has an alternative form written as 𠇿.
The character 藹 (short) is in the fourth tone (qùshēng), its sound being close to that of 櫻係反 (yīng xì fǎn).
The long *ǎi* (long *ài*) is pronounced near the sound of *jiè*;
the short *ào* (short *ào*) is in the departing tone and is pronounced near *wū*, with its alternative form written as 􆿑;
the long *ào* (long *ào*) is pronounced according to the character’s length, with its alternative form written as 􆿒.
The short character 𑀓 (ka) has the departing tone and its sound is close to that of the rhyme "jian" (鑑); its variant form is 𑀓 (kā).
The long character 𑀓 (kā) has the departing tone and its sound is close to that of "e" (惡).
Tripitaka Master Yijing states:
In the first three pairs, the upper [syllable] is short and the upper [syllable] is long;
in the latter three pairs, the upper [syllable] is long and the lower [syllable] is short.
These twelve *siddham* characters serve as the rhymes for the subsequent chapter.
Just as when using the sound of the letter *ka*,
one calls upon it by means of the twelve vowels—
*a*, *i*, *u*, and so forth— one produces the twelve letters *ga*, *gi*, *gu*, *ghu*, and so on.
Next, by means of the sound of the letter *kha*,
there arise the twelve letters beginning with *kha, kha, kha, khu, khu, hu*, and so forth. Next,
there arise the twelve letters beginning with *ga, ga, gu, gu, hu*, and so forth.
The subsequent examples follow this pattern.
First, write the twelve short *ka* syllables;
from the second syllable onwards, add the *ma-da* [suffixes].
This refers to the differentiation of characters by their forms.
By pronouncing them according to the Siddham vowels,
one recognizes the names of those characters.
The examples from *kha* down to *cha* are likewise so;
these constitute one chapter.
What was formerly called the "fourteen sounds" refers to this.
Immediately following the character *au* within the twelve characters of the Siddham alphabet, there are four characters: *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*;
these are formed by excluding the final two characters from the preceding Siddham sequence.
These are called the "boundary-syllables" (dhātu-akṣara); the remaining ones constitute the fourteen vowels.
Now, regarding the consonant-producing syllables, we exclude the four characters *he*, *li*, etc.
As for the body-text (the Siddham alphabet), it is also called the "syllabary. The character *ka* (迦) is pronounced with a retroflex final (*jià*) and a vowel near *jiāng*.
The character *kha* (佉) has the sound of *qù* with the lower tone, approximating the sound of *qù kě*.
The character *ka* (迦) has the light tone of *qú* with the lower tone, approximating the sound of *qí xià*;
in other countries, its pronunciation approximates *yí kě*.
The character *ga* (伽) has a heavy tone, pronounced as *qú* (渠我反).
The character *o* (哦) is pronounced with the lower tone of *yú* (魚下反), its sound being close to *yǔkě* (魚可反);
in other countries, it is pronounced as *jiǎng* (講反).
The separate entity is *karmada*.
The five characters above are dental sounds.
The character *ca* (者) is pronounced with an initial stop and a final *r* (止下反), its sound being close to *kya* (可反).
The character *cha* (車) is pronounced with the initial *chāng* and the final *xià*, its sound being close to that of *cāng kě*.
Its separate form is written as [the glyph].
The character *shè* (社) is pronounced with the initial *biāo* and the final *xià*, its light tone being close to that of *zuò kě*.
In other editions, the character for "sound" (音) is written with the lower radical as 丅;
the character 社 has a double pronunciation, the first being close to *cuōwǒ* (昨我反);
the character 若 has a lower pronunciation close to *ruòwǒ* (若我反).
In other countries, there is the sound *yǎng*.
It is formed separately as [the character] 壤.
The five characters above are dental sounds.
The syllable *ṭa* (吒) has a sound close to that of "zhuo" (卓) with a retroflex *ra* (反) suffix;
its separate form is written as *kha* (加麼多).
The syllable *ṭha* (侘) has a sound close to that of "zhe" (折) with a retroflex *ra* (反) suffix; its separate form is written as [the character 𑖿].
The character *ṭa* (荼) has a light pronunciation with the initial sound of *zhai* (宅) and the final sound of *xia* (下).
In other countries, it has a pronunciation with the initial sound of *nuo* (搦) and the final sound of *xia* (下).
The character *ṭha* (荼) has a heavy pronunciation, with a sound close to *dang-wo* (幢我).
The character *ṇa* (拏) is pronounced with a retroflex articulation, similar to the sound of *niè* (搦) or *niè-wo* (搦我).
In other regions, it is pronounced as *nuǎng* (拏講); its distinct form is written as *gamata* (加麼多).
The five characters above are produced by the tongue.
The syllable *ta* (多): the "da" (怛) is pronounced with a downward tone, approximating the sound of *da* (多) with a reversed final;
its distinct form is written as 􈍠.
The syllable *tha* (他): the "da" (他) is pronounced with a downward tone, approximating the sound of *tha* (他) with a reversed final.
The character *da* (陀) has a light tone with the initial *dà* (大) and the final *xià* (下); in other regions, it is pronounced with the initial *dá* (可).
The character *dá* (陀) has a heavy tone, with a sound close to *dá* (陀) and *kě* (可).
The character *nà* (那) has the initial *nà* (捺) and the final *xià* (下), with a sound close to *nà* (那) and *kě* (可).
In other countries, there is the sound *yina*.
It is written separately as [the character 𑀲].
The five characters above are throat sounds (*kaṇṭhya*).
The letter *pa* (􄖵): pronounced with a retroflex *ra* (𭽽) at the end, its sound is close to that of *pao* (波我).
The letter *pha* (􄗁): pronounced with a retroflex *ra* (破) at the end, its sound is close to that of *pao* (破我).
The letter *ba* (􄗍): pronounced with a final *ra* (罷), in a light tone.
In other countries, there is a sound for the character *ma* (麼) whose lower part is not pointed, which differs from the one [in this text].
The character *ba* (婆) has a heavy tone, pronounced as *bó wǒ* (薄我反).
The character *ma* (麼) is pronounced as *mò* (莫下反), with a sound close to *mò kě* (莫可反).
In other countries, there is the sound "mǎng.
The five characters above are labial sounds.
The character 􄗱 (ya) is pronounced with the *yào* rhyme; its sound is close to *yào* (with the final *kǎn*), and it is also pronounced as *zhī* (with the final *yǎn*), though this is an error.
The syllable *ra* (囉): pronounced with the tongue curled back, the sound is like *la* (曷力下反), a tripartite combination;
the syllable *la* (羅): the sound is close to *lo* (洛下反).
The character *va* (嚩): the lower part of the character is pronounced like *fáng* (房), with a sound close to *fǎng* (可反);
in older readings it was also pronounced like *huó* (和).
One source states that the lower part of the character is pointed.
The character 奢 (śa) is pronounced with the lower radical of 舍 (she), its sound being close to that of 舍可反 (shě kě fǎn).
The character 沙 (sa) is pronounced with the lower radical of 沙 (shā), its sound being close to that of 沙可反 (shā kě fǎn);
it also has a single pronunciation of 府下反 (fǔ xià fǎn).
The character *sa* (娑): pronounced with the lower part as "sa" (娑), the sound is close to "suo" (娑可).
The character *ha* (訶): pronounced with the lower part as "he" (許), the sound is close to "he" (可);
in one manuscript, the pronunciation is "he" (賀).
